operations.description: Discord's `message.edit(...)` - only the bot that authored the message may edit it (matches Discord's own real rule). Reuses UpdateMessageCommand the exact same way CreateMessageAsync above reuses CreateMessageCommand - no separate edit logic. A field the body did not mention is left off the command entirely, which Messaging reads as "leave the stored value alone"; a field that is present but empty clears it. Note that an embeds-only edit therefore leaves `content` as it stands rather than re-flattening the new embeds into it: overwriting the bot's own text is the worse of the two failures, and the structural embeds still travel on the update notification for clients that render them.

operations.summary: Autocomplete: the client is holding a dropdown open waiting for choices, so unlike every…
operations.description: Autocomplete: the client is holding a dropdown open waiting for choices, so unlike every other interaction this one needs an answer *now*. The bot's reply arrives on its own gateway connection as callback type 8, which may land on a different pod entirely - so the reply is parked in Redis and this request polls for it rather than awaiting an in-process handle. Polling with a short deadline (rather than blocking on a pub/sub subscription) keeps the failure mode boring: a bot that never answers costs one request its timeout and returns an empty list, which renders as "no suggestions" instead of a spinner that never resolves.

operations.description: Removes someone who has moved out, and cleans up everything they were carrying.  A household has no kick. <see cref="F:Guild.Domain.Enums.GuildFeaturePresets.Household"/> leaves the Moderation module off on purpose, which strips <see cref="F:Guild.Domain.Enums.Permissions.KickMembers"/> for everybody including the owner - so until this existed, a flatmate who moved out and stopped answering their phone could not be removed at all. operations.description: Registers a device, or re-registers one that already exists.  Re-registration is not a no-op. It used to hand the existing row straight back, which meant a client that had just minted a fresh Ed25519 identity keypair - the normal consequence of a keychain miss or a local state wipe - kept the server advertising the *old* public key and the *old* key packages. Every Welcome anyone sealed to those packages was then undecryptable by the only device it was addressed to, silently and permanently: the private init keys had gone with the wipe. So a differing identity key is treated as a rotation - the stale stock is purged and the caller is told to re-upload.

operations.summary: Unregisters one of the caller's own devices: the row goes, and with it (by cascade) its…
operations.description: Unregisters one of the caller's own devices: the row goes, and with it (by cascade) its key packages, its encrypted backup and its push tokens - so a handset that has been wiped, sold or signed out stops being handed key packages for new groups and stops being rung. Login sessions from that device are revoked rather than deleted; they are the audit trail the user reads on the sessions screen. Until this existed there was no removal path at all: `DeviceRemoved` was declared and never published, and a device's push tokens outlived it indefinitely. The cascade is the reason this is gated. Deleting the row takes the device's encrypted backup with it - the only cloud copy of its signing key - and did so with no device check and no re-authentication, which walked straight around `DELETE .../backup`'s own guard. Signing yourself out is free; removing a different device costs the password, which is also the case where the user is deliberately acting on a handset they no longer hold. The certificate is revoked rather than merely forgotten. It is a public 180-day statement peers have already downloaded, so dropping the server's copy changes nothing for them; see .

operations.summary: Binds the caller's session to one of the account's already-registered devices, at the…
operations.description: Binds the caller's session to one of the account's already-registered devices, at the cost of the account password. Why this route has to exist. Backup reads, backup writes and device-to-device transfers are all gated on which device the session was established from (C2/§L.7), and a session only learns that at `/connect/token`. Every session issued before that plumbing landed has no device, and so does every session from a client that does not send the id yet - so on the day the gate goes live those callers lose all of those routes at once, with no way back except a full sign-out. There is nothing to backfill from (see ), and a time-based grace window would simply switch C2 back on for a while. This is the remaining answer: pay the credential, keep the session. The password is not friction, it is the whole mechanism. Binding to an established device row - one some session has already been, or that holds a backup, or that is one end of a transfer - is exactly the move a stolen session would make to appoint itself the laptop and read the laptop's backup, which is why refuses it outright on the registration path. It is only safe here because the caller proves the account, and it grants nothing that the password grant at `/connect/token` would not have granted anyway - that route binds a fresh session to any named device on the same evidence. Refuses to re-bind. A session that is already some device does not become another one; letting it would turn one password into a tour of every backup on the account.

operations.summary: Reissues a device's certificate without re-registering it
operations.description: Reissues a device's certificate without re-registering it.  Any device holding the account identity key may issue for any of the account's devices, which is what makes a 180-day expiry cheap rather than a recurring lockout. A device that nobody is willing to reissue for stops being verifiable, which is the point of the expiry.

operations.summary: Throws away every key package this device has on file
operations.description: Throws away every key package this device has on file. The counterpart to a client-side MLS state wipe, and the one route that makes such a wipe recoverable. The replenish count is derived purely from server rows, so a device that destroyed its local store while the server still held ~100 unconsumed packages was told to generate zero - and every Welcome sealed to those packages was undecryptable by the device it was addressed to, with nothing to signal it. Clients must call this before re-uploading, not after. Consumed and last-resort rows go too: they are just as dead, and keeping the last-resort package would leave the device reachable through a key it can no longer open.

operations.summary: Requests a verification code by email
operations.description: Requests a verification code by email.  Always 202, with no body, for every caller. A code is minted and mailed only when the identifier resolves to an account that has an address and has not verified it yet; that work happens after the response (see <see cref="T:Identity.Application.Services.AccountEmailDispatcher"/>) so the two branches cannot be told apart by how long they take either.   Breaking for clients that read the old 200 / 400 "User already verified" split. There is no authenticated equivalent to preserve the precise answer behind: `/connect/token` refuses to issue tokens to an unverified account, so a caller on this journey is unauthenticated by definition and there is no session in which they could be told more. The honest client-side wording is "if that address needs verifying, we have sent a code".

operations.summary: Requests a reset code
operations.description: Requests a reset code. Always 202, whoever asks. The status code was already uniform; the time was not. Rendering the template and awaiting the Graph send only on the account-exists branch left a several-hundred-millisecond gap that answered the same question the response body refused to, so both now happen after the response - see , which also absorbs the delivery faults the old inline try/catch was here to swallow.

operations.summary: Confirms an address with the emailed code
operations.description: Confirms an address with the emailed code.  Unlike the request route this one cannot answer uniformly - the caller genuinely needs to know whether their code was accepted. So the rule is narrower: an unknown identifier is answered exactly as a known account with an unusable code is, and every unusable-code reason shares one body (<see cref="F:Identity.Application.Endpoints.UserVerificationEndpoint.CodeRefused"/>). An unknown address used to short-circuit to 202 while a wrong code got a 400, which was the same oracle in a different shape.   Breaking: an unknown address now yields 400 rather than 202, and an already-verified account 400 rather than 400 "User already verified".

operations.summary: Publishes the account identity key, or rotates it
operations.description: Publishes the account identity key, or rotates it. First publication is a land-grab, not a formality. It used to require no password, write no audit row and emit no event, on the reasoning that there is nothing to invalidate - but per §I.2 no account in the field has a key, so every account was one stolen session token away from having its cryptographic identity chosen by somebody else. Whoever publishes first is who every peer TOFU-pins, and every device certificate that peers will ever verify chains to it. That is the same power a rotation confers, acquired for less, and invisibly. It now costs the same password, writes the same audit row and is broadcast the same way; the event carries `isFirstPublication` so a client can word it correctly. A rotation is a security event: it invalidates every peer's pinning and every device certificate issued under the old key. It costs the account password, is broadcast to every device, and lands in the append-only audit log. Stated honestly: the server cannot verify the recovery credential. The contract asks rotation to require it, but the recovery key is derived from a passphrase the server never sees - so the password is the strongest thing checkable here. The check that actually protects peers is `rotationSignature`, made by the outgoing key and verified by them. A rotation that arrives without one is accepted and flagged, because the legitimate lost-every-device case cannot produce one either; peers then require an out-of-band re-verification rather than auto-accepting.

operations.summary: One device's certificate, for a peer verifying the leaf it vouches for
operations.description: One device's certificate, for a peer verifying the leaf it vouches for.  There was no read route at all. §H.4's unrecognised-leaf check is defined as "fetch the owner's certificate for that device and verify it against their pinned account identity key", and the clients duly call for it - and got a 404, which they correctly read as "that device has published none". So the check looked wired end to end and could never do anything, at any enforcement phase, no matter how far certificate coverage climbed. Exactly the shape of failure §I.1's rollout is supposed to be steering by.   Readable by any authenticated caller, like the account identity key it chains to and the revocation list it is checked against: it is a public signed statement whose only purpose is being verified by peers, and withholding it would protect nothing but an unverifiable leaf.   Timestamps go out as epoch seconds because that is what the certificate signs. The verifier reconstructs the signed payload from this response; handing it ISO-8601 would make every signature fail to reproduce.

operations.summary: A user's account identity key, for TOFU-pinning by peers
operations.description: A user's account identity key, for TOFU-pinning by peers.  Readable by any authenticated caller, exactly like a Signal safety number: it is public key material whose whole purpose is being compared out of band. `Version` travels with it so a peer can tell a rotation from a rollback, and `rotationSignature` so continuity from the previous key can be verified automatically where it exists. Where it does not, the peer must show a safety-number-changed warning and wait for a human - never auto-accept.

operations.summary: The account's revoked device certificates, for a peer to check a certificate against…
operations.description: The account's revoked device certificates, for a peer to check a certificate against before accepting the leaf it vouches for.  Readable by any authenticated caller, exactly like the account identity key it chains to: it is a list of hashes of public objects, and it is useless unless the peers who need to consult it can. Withholding it would only protect the revoked certificate.

Serving it on ViewChannel let any channel viewer external-commit straight into the group and skip the join-request review altogether - see <see cref="M:Messaging.Application.Services.MlsGroupService.GetStateAsync(System.String,System.String)"/>.

operations.summary: Welcomes waiting for one device, across every context
operations.description: Welcomes waiting for one device, across every context.  Passing <paramref name="deviceId"/> selects only that device's Welcomes. Reading never consumes - see <see cref="T:Messaging.Domain.Entities.PendingWelcome"/> for why consuming on read throws away a single-use init key whenever the join fails.   Omitting it no longer consumes anything either. The legacy branch used to stamp every Welcome for every one of the user's devices as consumed, so a laptop's poll silently destroyed the phone's only way into the group - unrecoverable, and invisible from both ends. That was the bug; requiring `deviceId` is a separate, breaking change and is gated on `MlsPolicy.RequireDeviceIdOnWelcomeFetch`. Fixing the loss now and breaking old clients later is the whole point of splitting them: a client in the field keeps working, and it stops destroying its siblings' Welcomes today rather than at its next release.   The cost of the non-consuming legacy branch is that an old client re-fetches Welcomes it has already joined, because it has no ack call to make. That is a wasted round trip. The old behaviour's cost was a device permanently unable to read a conversation.

operations.summary: Marks Welcomes consumed once the device has actually joined their groups
operations.description: Marks Welcomes consumed once the device has actually joined their groups. Scoped to `(UserId, DeviceId)`. Scoping by user alone let one device consume a Welcome sealed to another's leaf - which it cannot use, and which the owning device then never sees again. A client that sends no `deviceId` falls back to the `X-Device-Id` header rather than acking nothing: a silent no-op would leave old clients re-fetching the same Welcomes forever. With neither, the call is refused with a reason - the one thing that must not happen is acking broadly again. That header is not validated, and this route does not need it to be. It only narrows a delete-shaped write that is already scoped to the caller's own user id, so the worst a forged value achieves is acking the attacker's own Welcomes under someone else's device id - self-harm. The distinction matters because C2 was created by exactly this comment written one word stronger somewhere it was load-bearing: where the header decides whether the caller may read something, it must be resolved from the session instead (see `SessionDeviceResolver` in Identity), never taken off the wire.

Any member may, because in a DM there is no moderator - the two people in it are the only ones who could ever decide.

operations.summary: Adds someone to a group conversation
operations.description: Adds someone to a group conversation.  Same T0-2 rule as creation, applied twice over: the person being pulled in has to admit the caller under their own `DirectMessagePolicy`, and must not be on either side of a block with anyone already in the room. The second half is what stops a group being used to route around a block - adding somebody's blocked ex to the group they are in puts exactly the person they blocked back in front of them.   Refused on a two-person DM. Growing a 1:1 into a group silently changes what the other person thought they were in - that has to be an explicit new conversation, not a side effect of someone else's action.   For an encrypted conversation this only adds them to the roster; their devices still have to be admitted to the MLS group, which only a member's client can do. Until that commit lands they are a member who cannot read - visible to them, since they see the conversation but no history.

operations.description: The context is taken from the target message, never from the request body, and the caller is authorized against it - the same shape MessagingEndpoints.PinMessage uses. Previously this checked only that the caller was authenticated and trusted the DTO's ChannelId/ConversationId for the storage partition, so a user who had been kicked, banned, muted, or removed from a group DM could still write reactions into it (they are broadcast to every viewer and republished to Guild), and a mismatched context id wrote rows into an unrelated partition.

operations.description: Deliberately returns a bare IResult and no cascaded event. The MessageCreated for this send is raised by <see cref="T:Messaging.Application.Commands.CreateMessageCommandHandler"/>, which the InvokeAsync below runs - and Wolverine publishes a handler's other tuple member even when the caller asked for the first one, so returning a MessageCreated here too published a *second* copy of the same event. Everything downstream then ran twice: the realtime fan-out (a duplicate message and duplicate desktop notification) and, through Guild's channel path, a duplicate FCM/APNs push on every phone.

Fans out one MessageDeleted per removed message rather than a single bulk event: that reuses the whole existing per-delete pipeline unchanged (search-index cleanup, the MESSAGE_DELETE bot dispatch, the forum-post MessageCount decrement) instead of reimplementing each of those side effects in a bulk-shaped variant that could drift. Clients additionally get one aggregate realtime push so the UI can remove the whole range in a single update.

operations.summary: Hides or restores this message's link previews (docs/specs/message-previews.md)
operations.description: Hides or restores this message's link previews (docs/specs/message-previews.md). This is message state, not a per-viewer preference: the SUPPRESS_EMBEDS flag lives on the row every viewer reads, so dismissing a preview removes it for everyone who can see the message. That is Discord's behaviour and the point of the feature - the person who posted the link decides whether the card is shown. Suppressing also clears the generated embeds rather than only hiding them. Embeds an author wrote (a bot's rich card) are left in place and merely hidden by the flag, so unsuppressing restores them; a generated preview costs nothing to rebuild and should not sit in the row after someone asked for it to go.

The rows are deleted rather than parked at <see cref="F:Social.Domain.Enums.RelationshipStatus.None"/>. A lingering row for the pair would trip the "relationship already exists" guard in `POST /api/v1/relationships` forever, so an unblocked pair could never become friends - the block would go on costing them something after it was lifted.

Tears down whatever relationship existed first - an accepted friendship, a pending request in either direction - because a block that left a live friendship in place would keep the DM and call paths (both gated on friendship) open to the person just blocked.
